stem: What type does http_requests_total[5m] evaluate to?

options.note: Right. The [5m] turns the selector into a range vector, with a window of samples per series.
Without the brackets it would be an instant vector. The [5m] makes it a range.
A scalar is a single number, not a set of series.
The string type is currently unused in PromQL.

explanation: Appending a duration in square brackets to a vector selector produces a range vector: for each series, a range of samples back from the evaluation time.
hint: What do the square brackets add?

sources.title: Querying basics › Expression language data types

stem: In a range query (the Graph tab), which expression results can be graphed directly? Select all that apply.

options.note: Right. Range queries support instant-vector results.
Right. Range queries support scalar results.
Range vectors can't be the result of a range query. Pass them to a function first.
Strings aren't supported as range query results.

explanation: Range queries only support scalar-typed and instant-vector-typed expressions. Range vectors must be passed to a function, such as rate(), first.
hint: Graphs need one value per series per step.

sources.title: Querying basics › Expression language data types

options.text: Only series where env is exactly "prod"
options.note: Right. Regex matches are fully anchored, as if you'd written ^prod$.

options.text: Series where env contains "prod", such as "production"
options.note: Anchoring prevents partial matches. Use env=~"prod.*" for that.
=~ matches the regex. It doesn't match everything.
"prod" doesn't match the empty string, so series without env are excluded.

explanation: Regex matches are fully anchored. A match of env=~"foo" is treated as env=~"^foo$".

stem: Which query selects http_requests_total for the staging and testing environments, excluding the GET method?

options.note: Right. =~ with alternation for the environments, != for the method.
= is an exact string match, so this looks for the literal value "staging|testing".
The offset shifts time, which wasn't asked for, and the method regex is broader than needed.
Matchers go in curly braces. Square brackets are for range durations.

explanation: Use =~ for regex matches (such as alternation with |), and != for not-equal. Matchers go inside curly braces.
hint: Alternation with | needs a regex matcher.

stem: Given these series, which does http_requests_total{environment=""} return? Select all that apply.

options.note: Right. It has no environment label, and an empty matcher also matches a missing label.
Right. No environment label, so it matches.
Its environment is "development", not empty.
Right. No environment label, so it matches.

explanation: Label matchers that match empty label values also select all series that don't have that label set at all.
hint: An empty label value is the same as no label.

stem: Which of these selectors is illegal?

options.note: Right. It has no metric name and its only matcher matches the empty string, which isn't allowed.
Valid. .+ can't match the empty string.
Valid. method="get" can't match an empty value.
Valid. It matches on the metric name label, and that regex can't match empty.

explanation: Selectors must specify a name or at least one label matcher that doesn't match the empty string. {job=~".*"} is the docs' own example of a bad selector.
hint: Which one could, in principle, match every series in the database?

stem: Which expression correctly gets the sum of GET requests as they were 5 minutes ago?

options.note: Right. offset follows the selector directly, inside the aggregation.
Invalid. offset must come immediately after the selector, not after the aggregation.
offset is a postfix modifier on the selector, not a prefix.
offset doesn't go inside range brackets.

explanation: The offset modifier always needs to follow the selector immediately. sum(x offset 5m) is valid; sum(x) offset 5m is not.
hint: The modifier attaches to the selector, not to the function around it.

options.text: The 5-minute rate that http_requests_total had one week before the evaluation time
options.note: Right. The offset shifts the whole 5m window back by a week.

options.text: The rate over the past week
options.note: That would be rate(http_requests_total[1w]). Here the window is still 5 minutes, just shifted.

options.text: The rate averaged over 5 minutes, every week
options.note: offset is a single time shift, not a repeating schedule.

options.text: An error, because offset can't be used with range vectors
options.note: offset works with range vectors too, and this is the docs' own example.

explanation: offset works the same for range vectors. This example returns the 5-minute rate that http_requests_total had a week ago.
hint: The window size and the shift are separate things.

stem: What does the @ in http_requests_total @ 1609746000 do?

options.text: Evaluates the selector at the absolute Unix time 1609746000
options.note: Right. @ pins the evaluation time to a specific timestamp.

options.text: Shifts the evaluation back by 1609746000 seconds
options.note: Relative shifts are what offset does. @ takes an absolute timestamp.
Filtering by value uses comparison operators, not @.
@ is about time, not result size.

explanation: The @ modifier changes the evaluation time for an individual selector. The value is a Unix timestamp, here 2021-01-04T07:40:00Z.

stem: How do http_requests_total @ 1609746000 offset 5m and http_requests_total offset 5m @ 1609746000 compare?

options.text: They return the same result: the value 5 minutes before 1609746000
options.note: Right. The offset is applied relative to the @ time, whatever order you write them in.

options.text: The first is valid and the second is a syntax error
options.note: Both orders are valid.

options.text: The first looks 5 minutes after the timestamp
options.note: A positive offset looks back, relative to the @ time.

options.text: They differ because modifiers are applied left to right
options.note: The docs say the result is the same irrespective of order.

explanation: @ works with offset, where the offset is applied relative to the @ time. The results are the same whichever order the modifiers are in.

stem: An instant query evaluates at 12:00. A series' most recent sample is from 11:57, and it hasn't been marked stale. What is returned for that series with the default lookback?

options.note: Right. It's within the default 5-minute lookback period.

options.text: Nothing, because there's no sample at exactly 12:00
options.note: Prometheus uses the newest sample within the lookback period. It doesn't need an exact timestamp match.
Instant selectors take the most recent sample. They don't interpolate.
Prometheus doesn't fill in zeros. It returns the most recent real sample.

explanation: For each series, Prometheus takes the newest sample less than the lookback period ago, which is 5 minutes by default (--query.lookback-delta).
hint: How far back does Prometheus look by default?

stem: A target is removed from service discovery. What happens to its series in queries shortly afterwards?

options.text: They're marked stale and stop being returned for later evaluation times
options.note: Right. Prometheus marks them stale soon after removal, so they disappear from graphs.

options.text: They keep returning their last value forever
options.note: Staleness handling prevents that for normally scraped series.
Stale series return nothing, not zero.
The historical data stays until retention removes it. Only new evaluations skip them.

explanation: If a target is removed, its previously retrieved series are marked stale soon after. Queries evaluated after that point return no value for them.
hint: The term is in the lesson's staleness section.

stem: In current Prometheus, a range selector [5m] evaluated at time T includes which samples?

options.text: Samples with timestamps after T-5m, up to and including T
options.note: Right. Ranges are left-open and right-closed: the left boundary is excluded, the right included.

options.text: Samples from T-5m to T, including both boundaries
options.note: The left boundary is excluded (left-open). In 2.x it was included.

options.text: Only the sample exactly at T-5m
options.note: A range selects every sample in the window, not one point.
Ranges look back from the evaluation time, not forward.

explanation: The range is a left-open, right-closed interval: samples coinciding with the left boundary are excluded, and samples on the right boundary are included. (Prometheus 2.x was left-closed.)
hint: Open means the boundary itself is excluded.

stem: Which durations are valid in PromQL? Select all that apply.

options.note: Right. Units can be combined from longest to shortest.
Right. The classic example.
Time units can't be combined with a floating-point number. Write 1h30m.
Units must be ordered from longest to shortest.

explanation: Duration literals combine decimal integers with units (ms, s, m, h, d, w, y), ordered longest to shortest. Floats can't take units, so 1.5h is invalid.
hint: Two rules: integers only, largest unit first.
